articles.title: Ossoff wins reelection in battleground Georgia
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) will win reelection for another term in the Senate, holding off a challenge from Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), Decision Desk HQ has projected. Ossoff is leading with about 80 percent of the vote to Collins’s nearly 20 percent with 11 percent of precincts reporting. Georgia was one of the few legitimate…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) will win reelection for another term in the Senate, holding off a challenge from Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), Decision Desk HQ has projected.

Ossoff is leading with about 80 percent of the vote to Collins’s nearly 20 percent with 11 percent of precincts reporting.

Georgia was one of the few legitimate pickup opportunities for the GOP in the Senate, being a state that President Trump carried in 2024. But Ossoff’s reelection never seemed seriously in doubt as he consistently led in polling and easily outraised his opponent throughout the campaign.

Ossoff has been seen as a rising star among Democrats since he first won an open Senate seat in Georgia in 2020, helping to hand the party a narrow Senate majority. But his stock has been rising especially over the past year, and he has been the subject of increasing presidential speculation.

The senator has repeatedly brushed off the speculation, saying he’s not interested in running for higher office and is focused on winning reelection to his Senate seat. During a debate with Collins last month, Ossoff pledged to serve the entirety of his six-year term in the Senate if reelected.

“I have zero interest in running for president. I’m not running for president. I’m running for reelection to the Senate,” he said.

But now that he’s won reelection and the 2028 presidential cycle is around the corner, eyes will be on the senator to see if he sticks to that. If he were to run for the presidency, Ossoff wouldn’t be the first to do so after strongly ruling it out.

Former President Obama, whom Ossoff’s rhetorical style has often been compared to, famously said he didn’t plan to run for the office in 2006 before winning in 2008.

articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) is projected to defeat Republican Brent Andersen in the race to represent Florida’s 20th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Wasserman Schultz led Andersen by 60 percentage points — 78 percent to 18 percent — with 69 percent of the votes counted, according to DDHQ .

The seat had been previously represented by former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D-Fla.) for four years before she resigned in April. The district is home to a large Black voting population.

Wasserman Schultz’s bid for the seat came after GOP-led redistricting efforts in the state reshaped her current 25th District, making it far more favorable for Republicans.

Wasserman Schultz has served in Congress for almost two decades, representing Florida’s 20th District from 2005 to 2013, Florida’s 23rd District from 2013 to 2023 and Florida’s 25th District from 2023 to present day.

When she ran in the Democratic primary, Black Democrats had pushed back against her bid, arguing that her move not only disregards the district’s unique history and undermines opportunities for Black political representation, but is also a slight to Black voters.

But Wasserman Schultz had defended her decision to run, pointing to her years of experience and leadership roles in Congress.

“I know how to stand up for, fight for and represent diverse communities, and the feedback that I’m getting all across Congressional District 20 has been enthusiastic and supportive, because they know this is a community — this is a district that knows me. I’ve represented nine of the 14 cities in this district. They know me, and I know them, and they know that they want someone who has the seasoning, the experience,” she told NBC News’s Kristen Welker in late May.

She ended up defeating Cherfilus-McCormick, who ran for the seat again, in the August primary.

articles.body:
Republican Joe Strada is projected to win the race for Florida’s 11th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Strada, a small-business owner from Lake Mary, beat Democrat James Pericola to succeed retiring Rep. Daniel Webster (R-Fla.). Cook Political Report rated this race “solid Republican.”

Strada led Pericola by nearly four percentage points — 51.5 to 47.6 percent — with 51 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 7:13 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Strada started working as a handyman during high school and went directly into the trades after graduation. Through his HVAC, plumbing and electric company, he claims to have created thousands of jobs for his Florida community.

“Joe is not seeking a career in politics,” his campaign website reads. “He is running because Congress needs more people who have signed the front of a paycheck, built something real, and lived with the consequences of policies written far from the job site.”

Strada’s campaign website lists priorities that include investigating Congressional stock trading, enacting Congressional term limits and balancing the federal government’s budget. The site says Strada supports the Make America Healthy Again movement, finishing President Trump’s border wall and passing election integrity legislation.

Strada is a husband, father and grandfather. The Florida Republican was endorsed by GOP Reps. Randy Fine (Fla.), Jim Jordan (Ohio), Steve Scalise (La.) and Tom Emmer (Minn.) and Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.).

articles.body:
West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R) is projected to defeat her Democratic opponent Rachel Fetty Anderson to clinch her third term in the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The incumbent was endorsed by President Trump as well as her West Virginia Senate colleague, Sen. Jim Justice (R).

She is projected to win with zero percent of the vote reported, as of 7:33 p.m. EST.

“Senator Shelley Moore is doing a tremendous job representing the Wonderful People of West Virginia, a State I love and WON BIG in 2016, 2020 and 2024,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in May, issuing a “complete and total endorsement.”

Capito serves as the chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. She served in the House from 2003-14 and later became the first West Virginia woman elected to the Senate.

Capito’s father was governor of the Mountain State from 1969-1977 and 1985-1989.

articles.title: Michigan live results: 2026 Senate election
articles.summary: Michiganders on Tuesday will pick their next U.S. senator to serve for a six-year term, with two-term incumbent Sen. Gary Peters (D) opting not to seek reelection. The Michigan race is perhaps one of the most high-profile midterm contests this year, taking place in a state President Trump won in two out of his three…
articles.body:
Michiganders on Tuesday will pick their next U.S. senator to serve for a six-year term, with two-term incumbent Sen. Gary Peters (D) opting not to seek reelection.

The Michigan race is perhaps one of the most high-profile midterm contests this year, taking place in a state President Trump won in two out of his three presidential campaigns, including 2024. The Wolverine State was eyed by Republicans as a potential flip opportunity early in the cycle, and the nomination of public health official Abdul El-Sayed made them even more optimistic.

El-Sayed, who led the health departments in Detroit and Wayne County in the last decade, very narrowly won the nomination earlier this year over more moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a contentious and closely watched race. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow also ran in the primary and, at one point, led in some polls, but she dropped out before the election.

On the Republican side, former Rep. Mike Rogers is mounting a second bid for the upper chamber, after previously having fallen short two years ago against now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who was at the time a member of the U.S. House.

Polls close at 8 p.m. or 9 p.m. EST, depending on location within the state.

articles.title: Florida Democrat Kathy Castor holds House seat despite GOP redistricting
articles.summary: Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.) is projected to hold on to her Tampa-area seat after fending off a challenge from Republican Mike Beltran, and a bid by Republicans to redistrict her seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Castor led Beltran by 5.9 percentage points with 92.9 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as…
articles.body:
Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.) is projected to hold on to her Tampa-area seat after fending off a challenge from Republican Mike Beltran, and a bid by Republicans to redistrict her seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Castor led Beltran by 5.9 percentage points with 92.9 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 7:50 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Castor holds one of four seats that Republicans hoped to gain in the House through redistricting. Democrats now appear to have a fighting chance of winning all four of them.

Her victory also serves as a sign that the House majority may go to Democrats and that the party may hold a larger majority than once predicted.

Castor, who serves as a senior Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, has represented the region for nearly 20 years.

She faced a tough challlenge from Beltran, a former member of the Florida House of Representatives, after Republicans’ midcycle redistricting made the district more competitive for the GOP.

It was seen as a pickup opportunity for Republicans, with Beltran included as part of the National Republican Congressional Committee’s battleground seat program .

He was endorsed by President Trump in early September, but Beltran deemphasized his ties to the president in the general election, removing mentions and images of Trump from his campaign website that were prominently featured during the primary race.

Castor first joined Congress in 2007 as the representative for Florida’s 11th Congressional District. The 2010 redistricting cycle moved much of her Tampa-area constituency into the state’s 14th Congressional District, which she has represented for the past 13 years.

articles.body:
Republican Sydney Gruters is projected to win the race to represent Florida’s 16th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Gruters, who is the wife of Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters and was endorsed by President Trump even before she officially entered the race, will take over for her former boss Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.). DDHQ predicted prior to Election Day that Sydney Gruters was likely to win the seat.

Gruters led her Democratic opponent, Kelly Kirschner, 50.34 percent to 47.9 percent with 91 percent of the race called as of 7:57 p.m. EST, per DDHQ.

Gruters is a longtime House staffer and has worked for the Department of Agriculture’s Rural Development office. She most recently served as vice president of advancement and executive director at the New College Foundation. A self-proclaimed native Floridian, Gruters campaigned alongside Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) and retiring Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) during her campaign.

A secure border, controlling inflation and ensuring election security were listed as her top priorities on her campaign website . The website significantly features Trump through pictures and mentions of his political agenda.

“Sydney is ready to fight for democracy and stand with President Trump to ensure our elections are secure,” the website reads.

Gruters was also endorsed by Florida Sen. Rick Scott (R), House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and other members of House Republican leadership.

articles.title: Minnesotans leave their ‘I Voted’ stickers at Renee Good, Alex Pretti memorials
articles.summary: Minnesota voters are leaving their “I Voted” stickers at the memorial sites for Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two people killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Minneapolis earlier this year. The state was the site of one of the country’s largest immigration enforcement operations called “Operation Metro Surge.” The controversial initiative…
articles.body:
Minnesota voters are leaving their “I Voted” stickers at the memorial sites for Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two people killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The state was the site of one of the country’s largest immigration enforcement operations called “Operation Metro Surge.” The controversial initiative led to Good and Pretti’s killings, and rising disapproval of the Trump administration’s handling of immigration.

“I knew Alex Pretti,” a retired physician who placed a sticker at Pretti’s memorial site told The Guardian . “I just knew that he was a competent nurse — a really, really liked guy. And he was assassinated.”

“The country has humiliated itself by putting in a bad man, a very, very bad character … Today is a chance for America to say whether they support this kind of thing,” he continued, referring to President Trump.

Pretti, 37, was killed in January while filming ICE agents during the immigration crackdown in Minnesota. Last month, his family accused the Justice Department of protecting the ICE agents involved in the shooting along with refusing to provide evidence for ongoing investigations.

“Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable,” Pretti’s father, Michael Pretti, said. “Do your job and stop shielding Alex’s killers.”

“I felt like my vote felt a little bit more in touch with some of the things that happened earlier this year in the city,” a voter who placed his sticker at Good’s memorial site told The Guardian.

“So, I felt like it was just the right thing to do — to come pay some respects and attach my vote to what happened here,” he continued.

Good was killed in the beginning of January; a bystander captured on video the moment ICE agents fired multiple shots into her vehicle at close range. Her family and partner have filed lawsuits against administration officials, alleging in one filing that the operation was “designed to be a violent and discriminatory campaign targeted at Minnesotans on the basis of race and national origin.”

“Renee was one of those casualties,” the lawyers for Good’s family said.

images.caption: A person places an “I Voted Early” sticker at the Alex Pretti Memorial on Nov. 3, 2026, in St. Paul, Minn.

articles.title: Moody projected to win Florida Senate seat in tight contest with Angie Nixon
articles.summary: Incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) is projected to defeat democratic socialist Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Moody led Nixon by 0.7 percentage points with 84.3 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 8:03 p.m. EST Tuesday. Moody bested Nixon in a race the Cook Political…
articles.body:
Incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) is projected to defeat democratic socialist Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Moody led Nixon by 0.7 percentage points with 84.3 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 8:03 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Moody bested Nixon in a race the Cook Political Report said solidly favored Republicans. The senator entered the upper chamber last year after Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) appointed her to the role when Secretary of State Marco Rubio joined President Trump’s Cabinet.

The senator’s victory concluded a tumultuous race where Nixon, who won her Democratic primary in a shocking victory , called for Moody to be “ locked up and punished in jail ” over accusations she approved of mishandling taxpayer funds into a charity called Hope Florida while she was the state’s attorney general.

Moody was reportedly aware of the plan to divert the payment and “authorized” John Guard, her former chief deputy attorney general, to sign the settlement agreement, according to a sealed grand jury report obtained by CBS News Miami .

The Florida Republican campaigned on supporting Trump’s immigration agenda and “standing up for the rule of law,” according to her campaign website . She highlighted her legal background on the campaign trail, placing a heavy emphasis on law enforcement and public safety.

She painted her race against Nixon as one between “safety and chaos,” Florida NBC affiliate WPTV reported .

“This election is Freedom vs. Socialism,” Moody wrote on Facebook in August. “We cannot afford to have the radical Left take over our Free State.”

Trump endorsed Moody , praising her record in his home state and telling voters she was “doing a tremendous job representing the incredible people of Florida, a State I love, and WON BIG, in 2016, 2020, and 2024!”

articles.title: Ed Markey retains Senate seat in Massachusetts
articles.summary: Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) is projected to win his reelection campaign and continue his Senate career after 13 years in the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ. Markey, age 80, defeated Republican challenger John Deaton, an attorney and Marine Corps veteran. The victory in the solid blue state gives Markey his third term in…
articles.body:
Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) is projected to win his reelection campaign and continue his Senate career after 13 years in the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Markey, age 80, defeated Republican challenger John Deaton, an attorney and Marine Corps veteran.

The victory in the solid blue state gives Markey his third term in the Senate, where he has centered his work on climate change, health, education and economic issues.

In total, Markey has served in Congress for 50 years.

The win also came after a headline-grabbing primary between Markey and Democratic challenger Rep. Seth Moulton, who targeted Markey’s age in a failed effort to oust him.

In his primary win , Markey said his victory was made possible by young progressives and that this would be his last time running for office.

“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation,” Markey said in his primary victory speech. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it’s your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now.”

Markey’s win in the general election does not come as a surprise as the last time Massachusetts elected a Republican senator was in 2010 and previous polls showed him vastly ahead of Deaton.

images.caption: Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) reacts alongside his wife, Susan Blumenthal, after winning the Democratic nomination during a primary election night event, Sept. 1, 2026, in Boston.

articles.title: Juliana Stratton wins Senate seat in Illinois
articles.summary: Democrat Juliana Stratton, the lieutenant governor of Illinois, is projected to win the state’s Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ. Stratton was generally expected to win the safe Democratic seat, which is open as longtime Sen. Dick Durbin (D) is retiring. She will become the sixth Black woman to be elected to the Senate. …
articles.body:
Democrat Juliana Stratton, the lieutenant governor of Illinois, is projected to win the state’s Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Stratton was generally expected to win the safe Democratic seat, which is open as longtime Sen. Dick Durbin (D) is retiring. She will become the sixth Black woman to be elected to the Senate.

Stratton emerged from a bruising primary in March with help from Gov. JB Pritzker (D), who contributed $10 million to Stratton’s PAC. Her victory is a win for Pritzker, too, as he plots his political future and potential run for president.

Stratton, 61, has been the lieutenant governor alongside Pritzker since 2019. Previously, she was a state legislator from a Chicago-area district for one term.

As lieutenant governor, she has prioritized early childhood education, reproductive healthcare and criminal justice reform, among other issues. She began her career as a lawyer and later worked in criminal justice-related local organizations in Chicago.

Stratton is among the more progressive Democratic candidates for Senate this year. She supports Medicare for All, a $25 minimum wage and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

She has said she will not support Sen. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) for Democratic leader if elected and also pledged to take no corporate PAC money in her Senate race.

She had endorsements from several fellow Democratic senators, including Durbin, her soon-to-be delegation partner, Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.).

Don Tracy, the Republican candidate, did not have much backing from national Republicans, who were focused on competitive races and protecting Republican incumbents. Tracy mostly self-funded his campaign.

images.caption: Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton speaks during a primary election night watch party after winning the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, March 17, 2026, in Chicago.

articles.title: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas wins Senate seat in New Hampshire
articles.summary: Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is projected to win the Senate race in New Hampshire, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), keeping a crucial seat for the Democratic Party. The contest was considered a possible Republican pickup opportunity thanks to the party’s strong candidate, former Sen. John Sununu, who comes from a political dynasty in the…
articles.body:
Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is projected to win the Senate race in New Hampshire, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), keeping a crucial seat for the Democratic Party.

The contest was considered a possible Republican pickup opportunity thanks to the party’s strong candidate, former Sen. John Sununu, who comes from a political dynasty in the state. Sununu served one term in the Senate in the 2000s.

Pappas had secured nearly 61 percent of the vote with 22 percent of the ballots counted shortly after 8 p.m. EST, according to DDHQ .

But Pappas, 46, was also a strong candidate, especially after besting a democratic socialist candidate in the party’s primary . Throughout the campaign, he leaned into his record in Congress and his family roots in the state as the grandson of a restaurant owner who claimed to have invented the chicken tender. He is the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

The lawmaker also looked to capitalize on an unfavorable national environment for Republicans, tying Sununu to President Trump and the war in Iran .

Polls showed mixed signals for the months following the primary, as election handicappers moved it from the Democrats’ column to a toss-up and then back again .

While the Granite State has a history of ticket-splitting and has had a handful of Republican senators and governors in recent decades, it has also swung for Democratic presidential candidates reliably this century.

Pappas was well-positioned to capture that dynamic, as he has been rated one of the most bipartisan House members in the current Congress and the most bipartisan Democrat. DDHQ also gave the lawmaker an 88 percent chance of winning the race to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D).

In the lower chamber of Congress, he has served on the committees for Transportation and Veterans’ Affairs. Before being elected to the House, he was a state legislator and county treasurer.

Delaware Sen. Chris Coons (D) is projected to clinch a full third term on Capitol Hill, according to Decision Desk HQ.

He defeated Republican Michael Katz, a former Democratic state lawmaker. Katz ran for Senate unsuccessfully in 2024 as an independent.

Coons was first elected to the Senate in 2010 in a special election for the seat held by Democratic Sen. Ted Kaufman. Kaufman was appointed to the seat when former President Biden resigned to become vice president in 2009. Coons easily won reelection in 2014 and 2020.

On Capitol Hill, Coons serves as vice chair of the Senate Ethics Committee.

He easily fended off a primary challenger earlier this year in the deep-blue state.

articles.summary: Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Okla.) is projected to win his election for Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ. Hern, who announced his run for the seat after President Trump tapped then-Sen. Markwayne Mullin (R-Okla.) to lead the Department of Homeland Security in March, was the favorite to win in ruby-red Oklahoma. He defeated Democrat N’Kiyla Jasmine…
articles.body:
Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Okla.) is projected to win his election for Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Hern, who announced his run for the seat after President Trump tapped then-Sen. Markwayne Mullin (R-Okla.) to lead the Department of Homeland Security in March, was the favorite to win in ruby-red Oklahoma. He defeated Democrat N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a nurse and democratic socialist.

Hern notched endorsements from Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) and national Republicans, including Trump, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Oklahoma Sen. James Lankford (R).

Stitt selected Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.) to fill the remainder of Mullin’s term this spring. Oklahoma law dictates that the appointed senator cannot run for the full term.

In the House, Hern served as chair of the House Republican Policy Committee and is also a member of the Ways and Means Committee. He was sworn into the House in November 2018.

Prior to his career on Capitol Hill, Hern owned McDonald’s franchises in the state.

articles.body:
Former Alabama Rep. Jerry Carl (R) is set to return to Capitol Hill, Decision Desk HQ projects .

Carl, who served in Congress from 2021 to 2025, defeated Democrat Clyde Jones, an Army veteran, to clinch Alabama’s open 1st Congressional District.

Rep. Barry Moore (R), who currently represents the district, opted to run for Senate instead.

In 2024, Carl was pitted against Moore, who previously represented the state’s 2nd District, after redistricting put the fellow Republicans within the same district. The former lost to the latter in the state’s GOP primary by just a little more than 3 percentage points.

On the Hill, Carl served on the House’s Appropriations and Natural Resources committees.

The Alabama Republican was the heavy favorite to win Tuesday in the district that includes the city of Mobile.

articles.title: Former Hartford mayor secures House seat to replace incumbent Larson
articles.summary: Luke Bronin, the former Democratic mayor of Hartford, will win the seat representing Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District after ousting longtime Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.) in the primary, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ. Bronin’s win over GOP candidate Amy Chai was largely expected for the solid-blue district, which covers the area around the…
articles.body:
Luke Bronin, the former Democratic mayor of Hartford, will win the seat representing Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District after ousting longtime Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.) in the primary, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ.

Bronin’s win over GOP candidate Amy Chai was largely expected for the solid-blue district, which covers the area around the Constitution State’s center, including Hartford.

Larson, who was first elected to the seat in 1998, was among a group of incumbents criticized for their long stints in Congress. He served 14 terms in Congress and faced three Democratic primary challengers.

Bronin, who received the endorsement of the Connecticut Democratic Party ahead of the August primary , argued on the campaign trail that Larson is a “good man” but change is needed as the Democratic Party tries to find its footing under the second Trump administration.

Bronin served as the mayor of Hartford from 2016 to 2024, focusing on Hartford’s bankruptcy and affordable housing. Prior to this, Bronin was a senior official at the Treasury Department under the Obama administration, helping establish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

He later served as deputy assistant secretary of the Treasury Department for terrorist financing and financial crimes before former Connecticut Gov. Dannel Malloy (D) appointed him as his general counsel in 2013.

Bronin first got his start in politics working as Malloy’s deputy campaign manager in 2005, while attending Yale Law School in Connecticut. He later served as a Navy intelligence officer from 2007 to 2018 and was deployed to Afghanistan on the U.S. military’s anti-corruption task force from 2010 to 2011.

articles.body:
Democrat Patty García is projected to win and succeed her former boss Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.) in Illinois’s 4th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Patty García, the child of immigrants from Mexico, defeated three other candidates for the seat. She previously served as Chuy García’s district director and chief of staff, and has prior experience in community organizing.

Patty García racked up endorsements from figures such as her former boss and Democratic Reps. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), Robert Garcia (Calif.), Ro Khanna (Calif.) and Jerry Nadler (N.Y.).

Controversy has swirled around her campaign. In October 2025, Chuy García initially filed to run for reelection in the 4th Congressional District on the first day of the Illinois petition filing window. However, he later reversed course a few days after the filing deadline. The congressman then endorsed his former chief of staff, who had filed to run shortly before the deadline.

The House the following month passed a resolution condemning the congressman over the controversial timing of his retirement announcement.

images.caption: Maya Cazares, from left, and her mother, Rosita Cazares, talk with Patty García, Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García’s (D-Ill.) chief of staff, at Las Carnitas Uruapan in the Little Village neighborhood of Chicago, on Nov. 14, 2025.

articles.body:
Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) is projected to win another term in the House, thwarting the GOP-led redistricting that wracked the Sunshine State earlier this year, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Moskowitz defeated former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer (R), backed by President Trump, for the seat that became more Trump-friendly under the redrawn maps.

Moskowitz won 51.5 percent of the vote over Singer’s 46.4 percent, with more than 95 percent of the vote counted, per DDHQ as of 8 p.m. EST .

Florida’s 25th Congressional District, encompassing Broward County, was dismantled by redistricting, prompting incumbent Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) to run for reelection in the deep-blue 20th Congressional District being vacated by Democratic Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick.

Moskowitz, who represents the old 23rd Congressional District, ran for a third House term in the new 25th District, which stretches from South Beach to Delray Beach.

The moderate Democrat emerged the victor in an August primary against Oliver Larkin, a candidate backed by the Democratic Socialists of America who mounted a challenge from Moskowitz’s left — appeasing Democratic concerns that a more progressive candidate would struggle in the general election.

Cook Political Report shifted the race from “toss-up” territory to the “lean Democratic” label just weeks ahead of Election Day, offering a potential bright spot for Democrats seeking to stem Republicans’ redistricting gains in the state.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) championed the Sunshine State’s redistricting before the midterms, moving to expand the current 20-8 House advantage to give the GOP as many as four more pickup opportunities after a Supreme Court case shook up the national redistricting fight.

images.caption: Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) speaks to reporters as he arrives to the Capitol for a series of votes on June 5, 2025.

articles.body:
Maryland state Del. Adrian Boafo (D) is projected to win the race to succeed retiring Maryland Rep. Steny Hoyer (D), according to Decision Desk HQ.

Hoyer’s former campaign manager won the Democratic primary in Maryland’s solidly blue 5th District in June, setting the stage for his victory in the November general election. He defeated Republican Chris Chaffee, a perennial candidate.

The 5th District includes parts of Prince George’s and Anne Arundel counties, and it has historically been a reliable pickup for Democrats in the state.

Boafo was endorsed by Hoyer, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.).

The Democrat campaigned on lowering the cost of living, banning congressional stock trading, expanding childcare and education access, protecting the environment and investing in emerging technologies.

However, Boafo also faced criticism from elected officials within his own party for accepting millions of dollars in donations from pro-crypto super PAC Protect Progress and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s United Democracy Project.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Md.) accused these organizations of trying to “buy this congressional seat.”

Boafo is a native of Arlington, Va., and he earned his bachelor’s degree in government and public policy at the University of Baltimore before attaining his master’s in business administration from American University. He later worked as a senior director of government affairs for the tech company Oracle.

articles.body:
Donna Miller (D) will succeed Rep. Robin Kelly (D-Ill.) in the race for Illinois’s 2nd Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ has projected .

Miller is a Cook County commissioner and previously served as a board chair for Planned Parenthood of Illinois, as well as the vice president of Illinois Democratic Women. She is making a return to Capitol Hill with her victory, having done a prior stint as a congressional intern.

In March, Miller won the Democratic primary for the 2nd Congressional District, beating a crowded field for the safely blue seat in the Chicago area. She received notable backing from groups linked with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.) dropped her endorsement of the Cook County commissioner in February, saying she would not back a candidate with funding from “outside interests.”

Within the last few years, especially in the wake of Israel’s war in Gaza, debates have heated up in left-leaning circles about Israeli influence in American politics and military aid to the country. Some have even labeled Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide.”

Miller resides in Lynwood, Ill., and is married to former Illinois state Rep. David Miller (D). She has two adult sons.

images.caption: Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller, candidate for Illinois’s 2nd Congressional District, attends a forum hosted by the Democratic Women of the Southland Region, Feb. 28, 2026, in Chicago Heights, Ill.

articles.body:
Democrat La Shawn Ford is set to succeed longtime Rep. Danny Davis (D) in representing Illinois’s 7th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ has projected, beating out Republican opponent Chad Koppie, a retired Delta Air Lines jumbo jet captain.

Ford has served as a member of the Illinois state House, representing the 8th District, since January 2007. He went to Loyola University Chicago, where he played for the school’s basketball team before later becoming a teacher in the Chicago Public Schools system and then starting his own real estate business.

In the Democratic primary for Illinois’s 7th Congressional District this year, Ford battled it out against the cryptocurrency’s leading super PAC, Fairshake. He won his race despite the $2.5 million the PAC spent against him.

In July 2025, Davis announced that he would retire from Congress when his term is up. He has served in Congress for three decades, representing parts of Chicago during that time.

Davis was first elected in 1996 and has been a senior member of the House Ways and Means Committee in addition to playing a leadership role in the Congressional Black Caucus. He backed Ford in the bid for his seat.

Ford lives in the Chicago neighborhood of Austin and has a daughter named Tia.

articles.body:
Evanston, Ill., Mayor Daniel Biss (D) is projected to easily defeat his Republican opponent John Elleson for the House seat left open by retiring Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.), according to Decision Desk HQ .

Biss — a mathematician and former policy consultant — will serve Illinois’s 9th District, which represents parts of Cook, Lake and McHenry counties in the northeastern part of the Prairie State. The seat was left open by Schakowsky, who announced her retirement from Congress in 2025. She endorsed Biss in his bid.

He campaigned on strengthening worker protections, restoring competition to the economy and corporate accountability, according to his campaign website.

Before launching his House campaign, Biss served in both the Illinois state House and Senate, where he voted to pass protections for abortion rights and strengthen technology privacy requirements.

Biss’s bid was backed by Democratic Sens. Tammy Duckworth (Ill.) and Elizabeth Warren (Mass.).

During the primaries , he was notably attacked by Elect Chicago Women — a group aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — which spent $1.4 million against his campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings .

He faced controversy before his March primary victory when he admitted to going on a “handful of dates” with a former student while teaching at the University of Chicago in 2004. Biss’s campaign confirmed the relationship in a statement to The Daily Northwestern , noting the 20-year-old student had been enrolled in a course that Biss, who was 26 at the time, taught as a postdoctoral instructor.

Biss’s campaign added that Biss knew it was “ill-advised” and “ended” it at the time.

articles.body:
Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D) is projected to win the race to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, adding to the growing coalition of House progressives, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The democratic socialist had defeated incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), whom McKinney painted as an out-of-touch multimillionaire, in the primary. Running in a solidly blue district, McKinney’s primary win all but guaranteed he would be headed to Congress.

Throughout his campaign, McKinney gathered a wave of support from progressive members of the congressional Democratic caucus, like fellow Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and members of the Congressional Black Caucus.

The progressive PAC Justice Democrats chose McKinney as its first candidate it endorsed this season, saying back in April , “Donavan represents the future Democrats should be fighting for: working class people taking our power back from multimillionaires to deliver for everyday people. Always with the people.”

McKinney made his support for unions a core element of his campaign, having been a former member of SEIU Healthcare Michigan.

“I’m fighting for all my union family and for every worker to have the right to form a union, earn a living wage, and be able to provide for their family. That starts with making the ultra-wealthy like Elon Musk, Donald Trump, and Congressman Shri Thanedar pay their fair share — like the rest of us working people already do,” McKinney’s campaign website states.

McKinney’s win came after Thanedar distanced himself from fellow progressives, renouncing his membership in the Democratic Socialists of America following the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas.

McKinney has called the actions of Israel in Gaza a “genocide” and argued to “end the military aid and arms that America gives to Israel.”

images.caption: Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, Democratic candidate for U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan’s 13th District, speaks at a campaign rally for Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Aug. 3, 2026, in Detroit.

The race was projected as a “toss-up” in a district that slightly favors the GOP. President Trump carried the Sunshine State’s 22nd District by more than 10 points in the 2024 election.

A high school principal and teacher at the start of her career, she was appointed by Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) to serve on the state’s P-20 Council — a partnership among state, industry and community leaders to improve and assure quality of education. Dandiya campaigned on bringing down high costs, banning members of Congress from trading stocks and betting on prediction markets and for protecting personal freedoms.

Dandiya was endorsed by endorsed by a number of members of Congress, including Frankel, Reps. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.), Jill Tokuda (D-Hawaii), and Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.). Her priorities include lowering costs, banning congressional stock trading and protecting public schools.

articles.title: Democrat Jeremy Moss wins Michigan race to succeed Haley Stevens
articles.summary: Democrat Jeremy Moss is projected to win in the race for Michigan’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the official pick to replace Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). With 19 percent of ballots counted around 8:15 p.m. EST, he had secured 73 percent of the vote over Republican Ethan Baker, who ran…
articles.body:
Democrat Jeremy Moss is projected to win in the race for Michigan’s 11th Congressional District, becoming the official pick to replace Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

With 19 percent of ballots counted around 8:15 p.m. EST, he had secured 73 percent of the vote over Republican Ethan Baker, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary.

Moss’s win came as no surprise, with DDHQ rating him as the likely winner as early as August. The Cook Political Report also similarly projected the district would stay solidly blue ahead of Election Day.

Michigan’s 11th District had voted in favor of Stevens — who opted to run for Senate instead of reelection — by roughly 20 percentage points in the last two elections.

No stranger to politics, Moss has served in the Michigan State Legislature since 2015, becoming the Great Lakes State’s first openly gay state senator. He has also served as president pro tempore of the Michigan state Senate since 2023.

With his win, Moss will also be Michigan’s first openly LGBTQ member of Congress.

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) endorsed the Democrat as her pick to succeed Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens’s endorsement of GOP nominee and former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers over El-Sayed has captivated headlines in recent days.

Moss ran his campaign on tackling the cost of living, putting his support behind a “robust public option” as a means of achieving universal healthcare coverage. In the run-up to the election, he signaled his belief that the Democratic Party could be doing more.

“We need a stronger, bolder, tougher Democratic Party, one that does not show up to the knife fight carrying a pie chart,” the candidate said in an interview with the Advocate.

He also adopted a no-nonsense approach to addressing the issues while on the campaign trail, seeking to refocus topics away from cultural discourse like the discussion about transgender people in sports .

“There is no trans athlete in Michigan that is causing gas prices to spike,” Moss told the Advocate, likely referring to rising energy costs tied to the Iran war. “There is no trans athlete in Michigan that is putting up barriers to affordable healthcare.”

articles.title: Stigall set to replace retiring Graves representing Missouri in House

articles.body:
Conservative radio host Chris Stigall is projected to replace retiring Rep. Sam Graves (R-Mo.), beating Democratic opponent Josh Smead and Libertarian Andy Maidment in the race to represent Missouri’s 6th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Stigall, a staunch defender of President Trump, was seen as the top contender in the race’s GOP primary. He defended the Trump administration’s tariff policy, telling Spectrum News it was working and “we will see this level out for farmers in the future.”

“It is tough, and the thing that I know about farmers is, while they do know and feel these tariffs, are a very real hit, they also know that for decades they have been exploited by other countries that have been selling their goods on the cheap to us,” he continued. “President Trump is the first president, in a very long time, who came in and said, this isn’t right.”

Stigall campaigned on defending Second Amendment freedoms, expanding rural healthcare, delivering tax relief for farmers and small businesses and opposing taxpayer funding for abortion access, according to his campaign website.

He also backed a proposed amendment in Missouri that would remove the state’s constitutional protection for abortion access. The proposal was on the ballot Tuesday after voters approved it in 2024 , but a judge blocked parts of the measure .

“Protecting life means standing up for unborn children while also making sure mothers facing difficult circumstances know they have support and are not alone,” he said, according to The Kansas City Star .

His House bid was backed by Graves, Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

articles.body:
Democrat Stefany Shaheen, a health tech entrepreneur and daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), is projected to win New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Stefany Shaheen beat her Republican challenger, the Trump-endorsed businessman Anthony DiLorenzo, in the race to replace outgoing Rep. Chris Pappas (D), who left the post to launch a Senate bid.

DDHQ projected the race for Shaheen, who took 59.3 percent of the vote over DiLorenzo’s 40.7 percent, with 32 percent of ballots counted as of 8 p.m. EST.

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report regarded the district, which includes the eastern and some southern portions of the state, as “likely Democrat” from February 2025 up until a week ahead of Election Day, though both Cook and DDHQ placed Shaheen ahead of her opponent by just around 2 points.

The retiring senator’s daughter, a former Portsmouth, N.H., city councilor, narrowly clinched a Democratic primary victory in early September — defeating state Democratic Party Vice Chair Maura Sullivan, who also served as a top official for the Veterans Affairs Department during the Obama administration.

Shaheen received endorsements from Democratic Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and JB Pritzker of Illinois, sparking backlash from her GOP opponent. The Democrat defended accepting the governors’ support, saying in August, “Unlike Anthony DiLorenzo, who can write his own check to fund his own campaign … we’re working to build a campaign that’s of the people of New Hampshire.”

She went on to call out DiLorenzo’s endorsements, including from President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.).

articles.body:
Democrat Dan Koh is projected to win Massachusetts’s 6th District, taking over for Rep. Seth Moulton (D), according to Decision Desk HQ.

Koh, who previously served in the Biden White House, was widely expected to sail to victory after winning a tough primary battle earlier this year. He faced off against Republican Micah Jones, an Army veteran and attorney.

The Democrat was projected by DDHQ to win the seat with zero percent of the vote reported shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m. EST in Massachusetts.

The former Biden administration official had the support of a several high-profile Democrats from the last administration, including former President Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former Labor Secretary Marty Walsh.

Koh served as chief of staff to Walsh when he was mayor of Boston. Ahead of the 2018 election, he launched a bid for Congress but ultimately came up short in the Democratic primary against Rep. Lori Trahan (Mass.).

He later joined the Biden administration, becoming Walsh’s chief of staff again at the Labor Department and eventually moving over to the White House to serve as deputy assistant to the president and deputy director of the Office of Intergovernmental Affairs.

Koh takes over for Moulton, who left his forwent reelection to challenge Sen. Ed Markey in the Democratic Senate primary, failing to oust the two-term senator.

Democratic socialist Chris Rabb is projected to win Pennsylvania’s 3rd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) .

The Keystone State’s 3rd Congressional District has been labeled as one of the bluest districts in the nation, and Rabb will now succeed Rep. Dwight Evans (D), who has held the seat since 2019.

Rabb faced no Republican candidate in particular, and Dennis Mahoney was listed as an Independent on the ballot.

First elected in 2016, Rabb has served five terms in the Pennsylvania state House representing a majority Black, mixed-income legislative district in northwest Philadelphia.

Now, he will take over Evans’s seat in the 3rd Congressional District, made up of west, northwest, north and Center City Philadelphia.

Rabb has notably received endorsements from Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Illan Omar (D-Minn.), Summer Lee (D-Pa.), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and more. He was also endorsed by Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Haynes won what the Cook Political Report called a solid Democrat seat, defeating Republican Everett Jackson. Haynes previously won the…
articles.body:
The Rev. Frederick Haynes III, a Dallas pastor and Democratic House candidate, is projected to win Texas’s 30th District to replace outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Haynes won what the Cook Political Report called a solid Democrat seat, defeating Republican Everett Jackson. Haynes previously won the March 3 Democratic primary by a wide margin, receiving 72.62 percent of the vote, data from DDHQ shows .

Haynes is the lead pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church in Dallas, which has 13,000 members. In February 2024, the pastor replaced the Rev. Jesse Jackson to lead the Rainbow PUSH Coalition (RPC), the human rights group founded by Jackson in 1971. Haynes resigned three months later , stating that he remained “committed to honoring the rich history of RPC” and the pursuit of social justice.

Crockett backed Haynes, who has a long history of being a staunch progressive and was her pastor, The Intercept reported in February.

The two differed on some issues, notably Israel’s war in Gaza. The House Democrat voted to send U.S. military aid to Israel, but Haynes told Texas outlet WFAA in January that Christ was against genocide and that if “it’s in Gaza, he’s against it.”

“Every leader approaches things differently, and I greatly respect Congresswoman Crockett’s work and approach,” Haynes told The Intercept. “My worldview and my positions are deeply rooted in my community, and the struggles I see those around me experiencing on a daily basis. Our community is justice minded here in Dallas.”

The 30th District is made up of two counties, Dallas and Tarrant, and includes most of the city of Dallas. The Cook Political Report noted in 2025 that the district is one of the most Democratic in the Lone Star State.

articles.body:
Democrat Adam Hamawy is projected to win an open seat representing New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, keeping the safe blue seat in Democratic hands.

Hamawy, a surgeon and former Army physician, easily defeated Republican Gregg Mele, an attorney, to win the race to succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-N.J.). This was expected as Watson Coleman, an influential progressive voice in the House, easily won her 2024 reelection bid by 25 points.

Hamawy prevailed in a crowded primary field for the Democratic nomination earlier this year. He had gained attention previously in 2024, as he was among a group of physicians trapped in Gaza when Israel closed the Rafah border crossing.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), who credits Hamawy with saving her life after her helicopter was shot down in Iraq in 2004, intervened to help him and others get out.

Hamawy will be New Jersey’s first Muslim congressman.

articles.title: Cleaver clinches another House term after Missouri redistricting saga
articles.summary: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) is projected to roll to victory Tuesday, securing a 12th term in Missouri’s 5th District comprising Kansas City, according to Decision Desk HQ. Cleaver, a former Congressional Black Caucus chair, defeated Rick Brattin, a Republican state senator and former Marine who had allied himself closely with President Trump. Cleaver led Brattin…
articles.body:
Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) is projected to roll to victory Tuesday, securing a 12th term in Missouri’s 5th District comprising Kansas City, according to Decision Desk HQ .

Cleaver, a former Congressional Black Caucus chair, defeated Rick Brattin, a Republican state senator and former Marine who had allied himself closely with President Trump.

Cleaver led Brattin by nearly 46 percentage points as reported by DDHQ as of 8:15 p.m. Tuesday.

The race has been one of the most contentious — and most closely watched — of the 2026 cycle after Missouri Republicans sought to redraw the state’s House map with specific designs to make it impossible for Cleaver to win reelection.

That effort — part of a broader campaign, orchestrated by Trump, to help the GOP keep House control next year — would have given Republicans a 7-1 edge in the state delegation, up from 6-2 under the current map.

But critics of the effort challenged the changes in court, and after a back-and-forth legal battle, the new map was disallowed for this year’s midterms. Instead, Missouri voters on Tuesday were presented with a referendum to decide if the GOP map should go into effect after 2026.

Once the lines reverted to their current state, Cleaver’s victory was all but assured in a bright blue district. Former President Biden won the region by 26 points in 2020, and former Vice President Kamala Harris carried it by 23 points in 2024.

Those demographics made Brattin’s challenge a long shot in any environment, but even more so in a year when Trump is historically unpopular and the president’s policies — including global tariffs and the Iran war — have led directly to inflationary trends that are saddling consumers with higher costs on countless goods.

Cleaver, a Methodist pastor and former mayor of Kansas City, has a long track record championing traditional liberal causes, including a push to adopt tougher gun laws, expand healthcare access and preserve Social Security benefits. But he’s best known as an advocate for affordable housing, a position that should make him an influential figure in the next Congress, when Democrats are vowing to tackle housing costs as a top priority.

images.caption: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) talks about the Missouri Legislature’s effort to divide his district among three districts in an effort to flip his seat to Republican, at St. James Church, Sept. 7, 2025, in Kansas City, Mo.

articles.body:
Texas House candidate Tom Sell (R) is projected to win the race to lead outgoing Rep. Jodey Arrington’s (R-Texas) 19th Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ.

Sell, an agriculture lobbyist, campaigned in a solid Republican district against Democratic opponent Kyle Rable.

The Texas Republican won Trump’s endorsement, along with endorsements from House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

Sell previously worked for the district under former Rep. Larry Combest (R-Texas), “serving as his right-hand man when Combest chaired the U.S. House Agriculture Committee,” according to Sell’s campaign website .

After working to advance the 2002 farm bill, Sell returned home to Lubbock, Texas, and co-founded the consultancy firm Combest, Sell & Associates in 2005. The firm promotes itself as having more than 15 years of “defending agricultural interest.”

“A coalition of agricultural interests from across the nation sought out [Sell and Combest’s] counsel and leadership to protect the agricultural baseline in the 2005 Budget Reconciliation Process – an effort that was ultimately very successful,” the firm’s website states.

Arrington, who was first elected to the House in 2017, announced last November that he planned to retire from Congress at the end of his term. He took credit for helping Trump get the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed and for helping “fulfill his mandate from the people.”

“It just seems like a good and right place to leave it,” he said in an interview with Fox News last year, in explaining his announcement to retire.

The 19th Congressional District is nestled along Texas’s border with New Mexico and is home to the cities of Lubbock and Abiliene.

articles.body:
Former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas) is headed back to Congress after winning his race in redistricted Texas , according to a projection from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Allred was leading Republican Patrick Gillespie 80 percent to 19 percent with 74 percent of the votes counted as of 8 p.m. EST, according to DDHQ .

Allred vacated his seat to run unsuccessfully against Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in the 2024 cycle and later launched a short-lived bid for Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) seat in this year’s midterms.

Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) succeeded Allred in 2024 but lost out in an awkward Democratic primary runoff as GOP-friendly redistricting forced Democrats to play political musical chairs.

The new maps effectively merged Rep. Marc Veasey’s (D-Texas) 33rd District with Johnson’s 32nd District, creating a new 32nd District in the Dallas-Fort Worth area that favors President Trump by double digits, according to analysis by Dave Wasserman, the senior editor of Cook Political Report.

The reshaped 33rd Congressional District remained solidly Democratic, drawing both Johnson and Allred.

The primary results were a proxy win for Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) over state Rep. James Talarico (D), who beat her out in the Democratic primary for Senate. Crockett endorsed Allred, and Talarico backed Johnson.

House Democratic leadership, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and Rep. Suzan DelBene (Wash.), the chair of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, had also backed Johnson.

With his Tuesday win, Allred is headed back to Congress two years after leaving to try for the Senate, marking one of several potential comeback bids this cycle.

DDHQ gave the former lawmaker a 99 percent chance of defeating Gillespie ahead of Election Day.

articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) will win a second term as governor of one of the biggest battleground states in the U.S., Decision Desk HQ projects. articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) will win a second term as governor of one of the biggest battleground states in the U.S., Decision Desk HQ projects .

Shapiro’s victory comes as no surprise, as he was expected to coast to victory over state Treasurer Stacy Garrity (R). Just after 8:23 p.m. EST, Shapiro had more than 84 percent of the vote in early returns.

Polls consistently showed the incumbent ahead by as much as 20 points or more. Meanwhile, Garrity struggled with a lack of fundraising throughout the campaign, being overwhelmingly outraised and outspent by the Democratic governor.

In one sign of the writing being on the wall for Garrity, the Republican Governors Association never significantly invested in the race, focusing resources elsewhere in contests seen as more competitive.

The bigger question of the night in Pennsylvania is how big of a win Shapiro can attain. If he can win by a large margin, surpassing his 15-point victory from four years ago, Democrats may be in for a big night.

On the federal level, Democrats are looking to pick up as many as four additional House seats, targeting GOP Reps. Scott Perry, Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Brian Fitzpatrick. Flipping multiple of these seats could help Democrats pad their margin in a potential House majority in the new term.

On the state level, Democrats are hoping to win a trifecta for the first time in more than 30 years. The party currently holds a narrow majority in the state House and needs to pick up a few seats in the state Senate to flip it.

Winning control of both won’t be easy, but it’s viewed as at least conceivable for the first time in years.

Shapiro’s win also will likely draw more attention to him as he’s a speculated 2028 presidential contender . The governor has dodged questions about a potential bid previously, saying he’s focused on helping Democrats win this year.

articles.body:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is projected to win a third term leading the Prairie State, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Pritzker, a possible 2028 White House contender, defeated Republican Darren Bailey in Tuesday’s rematch. Bailey lost to Pritzker by more than 12 percentage points in 2022.

The billionaire Democrat ran unopposed in a March primary and was the favorite to win in the blue stronghold. He has made national headlines as a prominent critic of President Trump over the years.

Much of the focus on the incumbent governor in recent months, however, has focused on his future political ambitions.

His outsized wealth — from the Hyatt Hotels empire — would be a key asset should the governor run for president. As of late October, he had spent more than $38 million in the midterms.

Pritzker also put his thumb on the scale in the fiery Democratic primary for Senate earlier this year, with his pick, Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, besting two other Democratic challengers for retiring Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat.

The Democratic governor has trailed other high-profile Democrats, such as California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris, in recent polling around possible 2028 White House ambitions.

The Illinois Democrat has stopped short of completely ruling out a presidential bid.

Roy Cooper (D) is projected to win the Senate race in the Tar Heel State, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), notching a Democratic win in the seat being vacated by Sen. Thom Tillis (R). Cooper leads former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley by about 35 points with 51 percent…
articles.body:
Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) is projected to win the Senate race in the Tar Heel State, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) , notching a Democratic win in the seat being vacated by Sen. Thom Tillis (R).

Cooper leads former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley by about 35 points with 51 percent of precincts reporting.

Cooper has been favored to win for months, as a popular governor with high name recognition in the key swing state. His opponent was endorsed by President Trump but saw national Republicans shift their funding and attention away from him in the later months of the race.

Tillis announced his retirement plans in June 2025, a day after joining Democrats to oppose Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act over its cuts to Medicaid benefits . Since then, he has become one of the more outspoken critics of the Trump administration.

But he still backed Whatley and publicly worried about the advantage Democrats would have over Republicans due to unpopular Trump policies, such as the war in Iran.

Cooper, 69, was governor in the state from 2017 to 2025 after serving 16 years as attorney general. Previously, he practiced law and then was a state legislator, later rising to majority leader of the state Senate in the late 1990s. In all that time, he never lost an election.

As the state’s chief executive, he pushed for a sweeping expansion of Medicaid benefits and a slate of laws protecting victims of domestic violence, among other measures. Cooper also pushed for increases to teacher and state worker pay and state funding for infrastructure projects.

DDHQ gave the Democrat an 85 percent chance of flipping the seat ahead of Election Day.

articles.title: DNC chair says Democrats should repeal Trump tariffs, end Iran war if they win power
articles.summary: Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said Democrats should move to end President Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war if they take power after the midterm elections. Martin told NewsNation’s Blake Burman that exit polls are showing voters believe the country is going in the wrong direction and laid out the issues Democrats should address…
articles.body:
Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said Democrats should move to end President Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war if they take power after the midterm elections.

Martin told NewsNation’s Blake Burman that exit polls are showing voters believe the country is going in the wrong direction and laid out the issues Democrats should address if they take power over the next Congress. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) predicted before Election Day that Democrats are likely to win both chambers this midterm cycle.

“I think the first thing they should do is repeal the tariffs that Donald Trump put in place,” Martin said.

For Congress to exercise its constitutional authority over tariffs, it would first need to overcome an extremely likely presidential veto once it sends legislation to Trump’s desk. To reach the 67-vote threshold to overturn that veto, Democrats would need to convince a large chunk of Republicans to vote in favor — which would not be an easy task.

Martin said the second priority for Democrats should be ending the Iran war. The Senate has come close to passing a resolution to pull troops out of Iran multiple times, but it has yet to reach a simple majority threshold. That resolution would also be subject to a veto and would need 67 votes to overturn.

“Second is to end the war, which is driving up energy costs and fuel costs in this country at a time when people are already economically dispossessed and feeling a lot of anxiety,” Martin said.

Once they tackle tariffs and the war, Martin said Democrats should push to pass an agenda that tackles high costs, reforms the healthcare system and targets corruption. He said Democrats will work to end many Trump policies if they take the majority.

“I believe within the first hundred days, you’re going to see a very aggressive House and Senate to repeal a lot of the terrible policies that Donald Trump and his administration have put in place,” Martin said.

articles.body:
Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is projected to win Kentucky’s open Senate seat and succeed retiring Sen. Mitch McConnell (R), according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Barr defeated former Kentucky state Rep. Charles Booker (D) in what DDHQ, The Hill’s election partner, deemed would be a safe win for the Republican lawmaker. The Cook Political Report categorized the Senate race as a being solidly in favor of the GOP.

Barr led Booker by 3.9 percentage points with 38 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 8:26 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

Barr received a wave of endorsements from Kentucky and national Republicans, including from President Trump and GOP leadership in the House and Senate.

The president had asked business owner Nate Morris, another Senate hopeful, to “step aside” from the GOP primary and join his administration as a U.S. ambassador, which he accepted, clearing the way for Barr to be the nominee.

The president endorsed Barr on Truth Social in May, writing that the lawmaker “is a Strong Supporter of TERMINATING THE FILIBUSTER, before the Democrats do it (which they will, on Day One, if they get control of the U.S. Senate!).”

Barr was first elected to Congress in 2012, becoming a vocal opponent against former President Obama. He previously worked on Capitol Hill as an intern for McConnell and then later as a legislative assistant to former Rep. Jim Talent (R-Mo.).

McConnell was already expecting to retire at the end of his term, having announced that he would step down from Republican leadership in February 2024. But a fall at his Washington townhouse in June and subsequent hospitalization led to weeks of speculation about his health.

The lawmaker’s months-long absence prompted Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) to request proof of life and fueled speculation online, including after the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The influential Kentucky Republican released statements and photos showing proof of life, ultimately returning to Capitol Hill in September.

articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) is projected to defeat Democrat David Jolly in the Florida gubernatorial race , according to Decision Desk HQ.

Donalds, who has represented the Sunshine State’s 19th Congressional District since 2021, will succeed outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) in January. DeSantis is term-limited and could not run for reelection.

Donalds is leading Jolly by 0.8 percentage points with 93.4 percent of the vote counted as of 8:30 p.m. EST on Tuesday, according to DDHQ.

The three-term representative won comfortably in the August Republican primary , defeating Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins (R) by 20-plus points.

His win extends the GOP’s grip on the Florida governor’s mansion in Tallahassee by defeating Jolly, a former Republican who represented Florida’s 13th Congressional District for three years in the 2010s.

A Democrat has not won a governor’s race in Florida — long one of the prized swing states in presidential contests — since then-Gov. Lawton Chiles (D) defeated future Gov. Jeb Bush (R) in 1994.

When he is sworn in on Jan. 8, Donalds will become the first Black governor in Florida’s history and just the second Black governor of a state south of the Mason-Dixon Line.

Donalds will also join Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) as the only Black governors in the country.

But Donalds, who is of Jamaican and Panamanian descent, downplayed the historical stakes of his candidacy on the campaign trail, saying in March he has not “focused” on his race while in politics.

“It’s not so much about my race,” he told Jim DeFede of CBS News Miami . “I think [it] is more about the policies I support, the principles I stand for, commonsense conservative policies that have made Florida the envy of the other 49 states in the union.”

Before he even launched his campaign, Donalds had President Trump’s backing . Days before the congressman entered the race, the president said he “would be a truly Great and Powerful” governor of the country’s third-largest state by population.

But while Donalds praised DeSantis on the trail, the outgoing governor did not officially endorse his fellow Republican until September — after he won the nomination.

Donalds’s lieutenant governor will be Florida state Sen. Bryan Ávila (R). He is the third lieutenant governor of Cuban descent in the state’s history, following Republicans Carlos Lopez-Cantera and Jeanette Nuñez.

articles.title: Jesse Watters: ‘I don’t think we’re getting our $5,000 checks’
articles.summary: Conservative Fox News commentator Jesse Watters predicted President Trump will not be able to make good on his promise to send a check for $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. “I’ve looked at the numbers … it’s not a red wave,” Watters said while smirking during…
articles.body:
Conservative Fox News commentator Jesse Watters predicted President Trump will not be able to make good on his promise to send a check for $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“I’ve looked at the numbers … it’s not a red wave,” Watters said while smirking during Fox’s election night coverage. “I don’t think we’re going to get our $5,000 checks, and so the Democrats are having a good night.”

Trump had promised to have his administration send checks to every American if the GOP held on to both the House and Senate, a pledge that sparked widespread bipartisan concern about its feasibility and legality.

“The Democrats handed Donald Trump three major problems: the economy, immigration and crime … he solved two out of the three. He didn’t solve the economy,” Watters continued. “He has said short-term pain, long-term gain. To use a golf analogy, he didn’t come to lay up.”

Watters’s comments came during a Fox segment that featured Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, who said — after speaking with the president — he was “cautiously optimistic” about the GOP’s chances in Tuesday’s midterms.

Leavitt joined Fox as a contributor after leaving Trump’s White House.

“The reality of it is history is not on his side,” Leavitt said of the president. “The president has been pragmatic about that, but he still left it all on the field. If voters decided to get up today and turn out the polls, it will be a better night for Republicans, but that remains to be seen.”

The president posted on Truth Social several times Tuesday night complaining about Fox’s coverage of the election results, saying the network was spending too much time highlighting “Dumocrats,” which he argued would turn off viewers.

articles.summary: Democrat Jamie Ager is projected to flip North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The seat became open when Rep. articles.body:
Democrat Jamie Ager is projected to flip North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District seat, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The seat became open when Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) decided not to run for reelection amid his censure in the House over misconduct allegations.

Ager, a fourth-generation farmer, is projected to defeat his opponents, North Carolina state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom (R) and libertarian Travis Groo, according to Decision Desk HQ , with more than 60 percent of the vote and 64 percent of ballots counted at 8:30 p.m. EST.

The Democrat focused his campaign on helping western North Carolina recover from 2024’s Hurricane Helene, widening access to affordable and accessible healthcare, reforming the U.S.’s immigration system and securing protections for national parks in the Tar Heel State.

Edwards, who has represented the district since January 2023, said earlier this year he was ending his bid for a third term — two days after the House Ethics Committee recommended lawmakers formally censure him after he violated the “spirit” of the chamber’s policies on sexual harassment against staff.

Members of the GOP’s executive committee for the 11th District selected Balkcom to run in Edwards’s place, 85 days before Election Day.

Ager’s bid was backed by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who said Ager “brings a farmer’s sense of ethics to public service: care for what you’ve been given, think long-term, and leave things better than you found them.”

“At a moment like this, Jamie’s grounded, serious approach is exactly what we need in Congress,” Buttigieg added.

Ager notably distanced himself from the Democratic Party, writing on his campaign website that he has never been afraid to speak out “against his own party or taking on extremists,” calling himself a “mountain Democrat.”

“What I stand for is simple: I’m a Mountain Democrat. Always have been, always will be,” he wrote, according to the Asheville Watchdog , which Ager said meant “keeping our tax dollars spent here and not on wars overseas, defending our LGBTQ and immigrant neighbors and working to build a Western North Carolina that works for all of us.”

articles.body:
Democrat Helena Foulkes is projected to take over Rhode Island’s gubernatorial mansion, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Foulkes was leading with 56 percent of the vote to Independent candidate Ken Block’s 28 percent with 50 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 8:42 p.m. EST.

Foulkes, a former CVS Pharmacy executive, fended off a challenge from Republican Aaron Guckian and Block in the solid blue state. The Democrat notably ousted Gov. Dan McKee (D) in a September primary — the only example of a gubernatorial incumbent unsuccessfully seeking their party’s nomination this cycle.

A Republican has not won the governorship in the state since 2006, and Foulkes was the favorite to win Tuesday. She notched support from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

McKee’s primary loss was not particularly surprising. He is one of the country’s most unpopular governors, according to Cook Political Report, and Foulkes first ran against the embattled Democrat in 2022, losing by single digits.

The sitting governor has been under fire for his handling of the closure and rebuilding of the Washington Bridge. The bridge, which runs from Providence to East Providence, has been closed since 2023. His administration defended its approach, saying the thruway will reopen in 2028.

McKee ascended to the governorship in 2021 after then-Gov. Gina Raimondo (D) was tapped to join the Biden administration as Commerce secretary. He served one full elected term.

articles.title: Bean set to return to Capitol Hill after Illinois House victory

Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), according to Decision Desk HQ. Bean led Davis by more than 30 percentage points with 24 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Melissa Bean (D-Ill.) is projected to return to Capitol Hill after defeating Republican opponent Jennifer Davis for the House seat left open by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), according to Decision Desk HQ.

Bean led Davis by more than 30 percentage points with 24 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 8:46 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Bean previously represented an iteration of the Chicago-area 8th District until she lost a bid for a fourth House term amid the 2010 Tea Party wave. She credited the loss to her continual defense of the Affordable Care Act while she served in Congress, according to her campaign website .

She competed in a crowded Democratic primary in March against seven other candidates and garnered around 4,000 more votes than Junaid Ahmed, who came in second. Her primary win and campaign was backed by Elect Chicago Women — aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — and other AI-focused lobby groups , according to Federal Election Commission filings .

Bean campaigned on strengthening the middle class, greater oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and providing affordable and high-quality healthcare.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) and former Illinois Secretary of State Jesse White endorsed Bean in her bid for the open House seat . Krishnamoorthi unsuccessfully ran for Senate.

In her first stint in Congress, Bean, a moderate, was a part of the New Democrat Coalition, which is described as a group of “forward-thinking Democrats who are committed to pro-economic growth, pro-innovation, and fiscally responsible policies.”

She worked with Pelosi on ObamaCare, along with Wall Street reform and the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, which extended the time period for individuals to file charges of alleged pay discrimination under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act.

After leaving Congress, Bean worked in the private sector at finance firms including JPMorgan Chase and Mesirow Financial before deciding to run again.
