articles.title: Leavitt says Trump ‘remains cautiously optimistic’
articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Tuesday evening on Fox News she recently spoke with President Trump and that he “remains cautiously optimistic” about the midterm election results. “One thing he said is he left it all on the field,” she said. “And that is certainly true. He went 30-for-30 over the course…
articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Tuesday evening on Fox News she recently spoke with President Trump and that he “remains cautiously optimistic” about the midterm election results.

“One thing he said is he left it all on the field,” she said. “And that is certainly true. He went 30-for-30 over the course of the last month. He held 15 telerallies just yesterday alone. I’m talking to my friends at the White House, set up in the war room tonight as well.”

Leavitt said the White House is closely following the Election Day vote turnout, noting a higher percentage of Democrats than Republicans tend to vote by mail.

“If voters decided to wake up this morning and turn out to the polls, it would be a better night for Republicans than I think some of the pundits had predicted,” she said. “That still has yet to be seen.”

Republicans have already been hit by several losses in states on Tuesday evening, including in red strongholds in Florida and North Carolina.

Decision Desk HQ predicted in a Tuesday morning forecast there was an 84 percent chance Democrats regained control of the House, while Democrats had a 64 percent probability of retaking the Senate.

The president has repeatedly urged Americans to vote as if he were “on the ballot,” despite his waning job approval ratings amid rising costs of living and the Iran war .

In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) defeated GOP nominee John E. Sununu, securing a Democratic seat in the Senate vacated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Leavitt, who launched an unsuccessful attempt to oust Pappas from his House seat in 2022, called the election result “a disappointing loss for our state.”

“Got to give it to him, he is a good candidate for the Democrats,” Leavitt said. “He appears like a moderate, but when he gets into office, he votes with the far left of his party.”

articles.body:
Melat Kiros, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is projected to win the race to represent Colorado’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Kiros, 29, defeated Republican Christy Peterson, Libertarian Chad Humphrey, Critter Milton of the Unity Party and Independent candidate Shimon Blau. Her victory reflects a broader wave of younger, progressive Democrats who launched congressional bids this year, seeking to usher in a new generation of leadership within the party.

DDHQ projected the race at 9 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Kiros is a Ph.D. student at the University of Colorado Denver School of Public Affairs who quickly rose to prominence after she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (Colo.) in the Democratic primary this summer.

She received the backing of several high-profile progressive figures and groups, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), End Citizens United and Justice Democrats.

Kiros received a law degree from the University of Notre Dame in 2022.

She was fired from the law firm Sidley Austin in 2023 after she wrote a letter directed at U.S. law firms on her Substack in which she disputed the notion that it was antisemitic to call “for the elimination of the Israeli state.” She refused to take down the letter.

Kiros’s platform includes “Medicare for All,” universal childcare and eldercare and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Her campaign website says that she also supports an ultramillionaire tax on people with a net worth of more than $50 million.

articles.body:
New York Assembly member Claire Valdez (D) is projected to win the state’s 7th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The victory comes with little surprise, as Valdez consistently polled decisively ahead of her Republican challenger Melvin Rivera after winning the Democratic primary in June. She will replace retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez (D), who has held the seat in New York City since 2013.

Ahead of the primary, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and the Democratic Socialists of America endorsed Valdez over her challenger, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso — who had Velázquez’s backing.

Democrats have held on to the majority-minority district , which encompasses portions of Brooklyn and Queens, for the past century. In 2024, the then-Democratic supermajority in the state Legislature redrew the Empire State’s congressional maps, giving their party a slight boost in the 7th District.

In her time as a State Assembly member, Valdez has championed affordability measures and “tax the rich” campaigns — drawing on her background as a union leader .

Her GOP opponent describes himself as a “community activist” of more than three decades, having focused his advocacy on housing issues and renter rights.

articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is projected to sail to victory in New York City on Tuesday, easily beating back a symbolic challenge from Lewis Mizrahi, a Republican data analyst who never stood a chance in the deep-blue Brooklyn district, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Jeffries has been the top House Democrat since 2023, when Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) stepped out of that seat to clear the way for a younger generation of party leaders. And if Democrats flip control of the chamber in this year’s midterms, Jeffries — the first Black lawmaker to lead either party in Congress — is expected to make history again by becoming the country’s first Black Speaker.

From that perch, Jeffries has promised to move an ambitious legislative agenda through the lower chamber, including bills to reverse GOP Medicaid cuts, curb the high cost of living, and end the war in Iran. Those proposals have no chance of becoming law with President Trump in the White House, but they will provide Democrats with campaign ammunition heading into the 2028 presidential election.

Jeffries is also vowing to provide a check on the Trump administration by launching a host of investigations into the president and his inner circle, including probes into Trump’s efforts to use the office to prosecute political enemies and pardon loyalists convicted of violent crimes. That potentially sets the stage for explosive clashes between the House and White House over the next two years.

Jeffries will have his challenges. The House caucus is a diverse group, and party leaders will be forced to balance between the sometimes competing interests of centrist lawmakers from battleground districts and liberal rabble-rousers fighting for far-left policies, including an incoming group affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Indeed, Jeffries’s greatest challenge this midterm cycle was not from Republicans, but from liberal Democrats who think he’s been too gentle in confronting Trump through the first half of the president’s second term.

Last year, Chi Ossé, a young member of the New York City Council and a member of the DSA, mulled a primary challenge against Jeffries for that reason. Ossé was encouraged by the success of Zohran Mamdani, another DSA member who won the race for New York City mayor in November 2025.

Members of New York’s DSA, however, declined to endorse Ossé in the race, and he quickly dropped his bid, clearing the way for Jeffries to win an eighth term without an internal challenge.

articles.body:
Former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander is projected to win an open House seat after successfully ousting the incumbent in the primary earlier this year, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Lander easily defeated Republican Jennifer Moore, a party operative, to hold the seat for Democrats in the safe blue district. A close ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), Lander defeated Rep. Dan Goldman (N.Y.) in the Democratic primary in June, one of a string of successes for progressive candidates in those primaries.

Goldman has been a reliable Democratic vote during his two terms in the House but came under fire from the left over his support for Israel.

Lander highlighted his opposition to sending additional aid to Israel and positioned himself to Goldman’s left, easily beating the incumbent by more than 25 percentage points this summer.

After winning his party’s nod, Lander was seen as a shoo-in to represent the district based in Manhattan and Brooklyn.
